9.0.0.en: Gird up your loins: to gird the loins is to put on clothing around the waist and below it, that is, a person putting on his clothes in preparation for a journey.

9.0.1.en: Box (vial): a small vessel in which the oil of anointing is kept; the oil may also be put in the horn of an animal.

9.0.2.en: Ramoth Gilead: a city located east of the river Jordan near the river Jabbok, in the portion of the tribe of Gad, and given to the Levites. It is one of the cities of refuge, and there were many wars between the Arameans and the children of Israel to take possession of it.

9.0.3.en: God had commanded Elijah to anoint Hazael king over Aram (1 Kgs 19:15-17), and this was done at the hand of Elisha, who did not anoint him with oil, because he was a Gentile who would not understand the meaning of anointing, but informed him of it (ch. 8:13). God also commanded Elijah to anoint Jehu king over Israel, and this is now done through Elisha, who sends one of the sons of the prophets with a vial of oil to Jehu, who was staying in Ramoth Gilead. God likewise commanded Elijah to anoint Elisha as prophet in his place, and this was done at Elijah's prayer, when the Spirit of God came upon Elisha in a double portion, just before Elijah's ascent into heaven (ch. 2:9-11). It is noted that Elijah did not carry out God's word at its time, because the appropriate time in God's providence had not yet come. And the carrying out of the divine command comes not only through Elijah himself but can be through his spiritual sons, like Elisha, or one of Elisha's disciples. Ahab repented when Elijah rebuked him, so God postponed his punishment to the days of his descendants, and this was by way of Hazael and Jehu, who were to be anointed after Elijah's ascent. From this it is understood that Elijah and Elisha and their sons from the sons of the prophets are one thing in God's sight, because the one Spirit of God is working in them.

9.1.0.en: Elisha charged one of the sons of the prophets, whom he sent to Ramoth Gilead, to look for Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi, and he would find him gathered among his brethren, the commanders of the army. He was to bring him into an inner room in the house, so that no one would see or hear him, and anoint him there as king. Jehoshaphat the father of Jehu is of course different from Jehoshaphat king of Judah. Because the anointing of Jehu was a grave matter, as we shall learn, for he would destroy and kill others, Elisha asked this prophet to do it in complete secrecy, going from room to room. Elisha did not go himself, because Elisha was a well-known person, and his going would raise questions in the whole city, and he could not anoint Jehu in secret. Elisha did not tell this prophet what to say to Jehu but contented himself with commanding him to anoint him, because God had commanded him only this, and God would give the words to this prophet, who would tell Jehu what was required of him. Here the obedience of the prophet Elisha to God appears: he does not interfere in His arrangements or His division of the work, that is, God wanted to tell the prophet Himself what to say to Jehu, and Elisha did not command him to say anything. Jewish tradition says that this prophet was the prophet Jonah. In this Elisha completes God's command to Elijah to anoint Jehu king (1 Kgs 19:15-17).

9.2.0.en: Elisha also commanded the son of the prophets, when he was alone with Jehu, to pour the oil on his head and inform him that he had become king over Israel, and then to flee at once, for fear for his life. For if there were among the army commanders anyone loyal to King Jehoram, he would of course kill the prophet; or if Jehu himself were loyal to Jehoram, considering himself only one of his army's commanders, he might rush and kill this prophet. That is, he was not to give Jehu a chance to think and speak with any of the commanders. Although God is able to protect His children, He asks them to do what is within their power, and then to rely on Him, and He will not leave them.

9.2.1.en: Be obedient to God's commands, and fulfill your responsibilities and your service, however difficult they may seem, trusting in God's protection of you, for He is responsible for you and works through you, so do not be troubled.

9.3.0.en: The young prophet went to Ramoth Gilead and entered where the army commanders were gathered. He addressed Jehu, saying, "I have an errand to thee, O captain." Jehu asked him whom he meant by his words, and he told him that it was he, that is, Jehu, who was meant. Perhaps Jehu asked the prophet whether he wanted to speak to all the commanders or to him alone, because he felt that prophets bring tidings of good news, so that he would not appear in the commanders' eyes to be monopolizing the good news; and when the prophet confirmed to him that he wanted him, he obeyed.

9.4.0.en: Jehu arose and went in to where he could be alone with the prophet, and the prophet quickly poured the oil on Jehu's head, saying, "Thus saith the LORD, I have chosen you king over Israel." God told Jehu that He was setting him over His people, so God still feels that Israel is His people, although they mix His worship with the worship of idols, but in His fatherhood He sends them prophets and anoints a king for them to destroy those who support the worship of idols, namely Ahab and his descendants.

9.5.0.en: The young prophet declares to Jehu the harsh judgment that he must carry out upon the house of Ahab.

9.5.1.en: He calls Ahab his master, because Jehu was in Ahab's service (v. 25), and then in that of his descendants after him, Ahaziah and Jehoram. The reason for this judgment is the way in which the king, on the counsel of his wife Jezebel, treated the servants of the Lord and His prophets, for he persecuted Elisha the prophet of God and all the sons of the prophets, and at the same time encouraged the worship of idols and the prophets of Baal.

9.5.2.en: If this prophet who anointed Jehu is Jonah, then he had heard Elijah when he declared to Ahab that God would destroy his descendants for his evil and theirs, and he now proclaims to Jehu the command of God, which he had earlier heard from the mouth of Elijah his teacher (1 Kgs 21:21, 22). Strangely, we read in the book of Hosea (Hos 1:4) and understand God's anger against Jehu for destroying the descendants of Ahab, because he destroyed them with brutality and for his own sake, that is, to secure his kingdom, and not merely in carrying out God's commands. God wants us to obey His commandments and not to add anything to them of our own thoughts and evils.

9.6.0.en: The prophet informed him that he must destroy every male in the house of Ahab ("him that pisseth against the wall"), without sparing anyone ("him that is shut up and left"), that is, the little ones who are in the houses, or the grown ones who move freely everywhere. He must make the fate of the house of Ahab like the fate of the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat (1 Kgs 14:10) and like the fate of the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah (1 Kgs 16:3, 4), that is, destroy them completely, because these three, they and their descendants, were very wicked, and God destroyed them.

9.7.0.en: The sentence was likewise that the dogs would devour Jezebel in the field of Jezreel and she would find no one to bury her.

9.7.1.en: As soon as the prophet finished speaking, he opened the door and hurried away. God's punishment of the proud and wicked Jezebel is that she not be buried with honor in a special tomb as queens are, but that her corpse be thrown out for the dogs to lick up her blood, as a lesson to the wicked, so that they do not persist in their evil but repent.

9.8.s.en: (2) The proclamation of Jehu as king

9.8.0.en: After the prophet fled, Jehu came out of the inner room and sat among the army commanders, the servants of the king, and they asked him what this prophet wanted and called him a madman, because the king and his court, on account of their evils and their distance from God, despised the prophets and considered them mad. Perhaps also the prophet, when he came in, was somewhat agitated because of the difficulty of the mission, so they described him as mad.

9.8.1.en: And they said to him, "Did he come in peace?" But Jehu tried to evade answering and to hide the matter; perhaps at first he was afraid to declare himself king, lest the army commanders oppose him because of their loyalty to King Jehoram. Their asking about the reason for this prophet's visit and their saying whether he came in peace or not showed that, despite their contempt for him, inwardly they felt the power of God in His prophets, so within them, along with curiosity, there was fear of what news this prophet was bringing.

9.8.2.en: The word of God may appear in the eyes of the world to be madness, and they despise it. So stand firm in the word of God with true faith and do not doubt because of their opposition to you, for they are troubled inside, and if they see your steadfastness they will back down, and even believe.

9.9.0.en: When the army commanders saw the oil running down on Jehu's head, they were sure that Jehu was hiding the truth from them, so they said to him, "You are lying to us; tell us the truth." Because they knew that oil is poured only on the heads of kings, prophets and priests, they suspected that Jehu had been anointed king. Before this open confrontation Jehu could not hide what had happened, and he informed them that the prophet had anointed him king and told them all that the prophet had said to him.

9.10.1.en: Each one of them hurried to spread his garment on the top of the stairs in the place where he stood, and they blew the trumpets, proclaiming, "Jehu is king." Thus God put into the hearts of these commanders a fear of Jehu, and perhaps they were troubled by Ahab and his descendants and their evils, so they declared their submission in the manner known at that time, which was for a person to take off his garment and place it under the feet of the one to whom he submits, as the disciples and followers of Christ did when He entered Jerusalem (Mt 21:8). The blowing of the trumpet is known among the Jews at the proclamation of the reign of a new king (1 Kgs 1:34). In this we see that God turns everything to the accomplishment of His purposes: the commanders who could have opposed Jehu submit to him so quickly, in addition to the fact that King Jehoram king of Israel was recovering in Jezreel alone, without his soldiers, while the soldiers were in Ramoth Gilead, which made it easy to proclaim Jehu king in the midst of the army.

9.11.0.en: Thus Jehu became king over Israel and declared his rebellion against Joram, especially as Joram had placed a large division of the army in Ramoth Gilead to guard it, lest Hazael king of Aram attack it, which helped Jehu to proclaim his kingship and the army's submission to him, so that he was able to take control of the kingdom easily by the power of the army.

9.12.0.en: Jehoram king of Israel was spending a period of rest and recovery in Jezreel, after being wounded in his battle with Hazael king of Aram. Meanwhile Jehu declared himself king in Ramoth Gilead, and with human wisdom and cleverness he said to the many officers and soldiers who were with him in Ramoth, "If it be your minds, then let none go forth nor escape out of the city to go to tell it in Jezreel to King Jehoram." In this he shares the responsibility with them, so that if the plan of his kingship fails, they would all be condemned before King Jehoram. He also wanted to frighten them so that they would prevent anyone from informing King Jehoram, to make it easy for him to kill Jehoram king of Israel suddenly. But unfortunately this shows a lack of faith in the power of God that supported him; it was God who had anointed him and was able to support him, but he relied on his own strength and cleverness, so there was inside him a fear that his attempt would fail.

9.13.0.en: Jehu rode in his chariot toward Jezreel, where Joram lay recovering from his wound. Ahaziah king of Judah was visiting him to see how he was. So to the very last the kings of Judah, in the person of Ahaziah, were tied to the wicked kings of Israel, and this wicked tie brought loss upon the kings of Judah, because it drew them away from God, so He was angry with them, and it benefited the kings of Israel in their wars. Every association with the wicked benefits the wicked by increasing their material strength, and corrupts the righteous by drawing them away from God Himself.

9.14.0.en: As was customary at that time, a watchman would stand on a high tower to watch for any military movements or others that threatened the camp he protected, so that the soldiers would be on guard before the enemy came and took them by surprise. A watchman was standing on a tower in Jezreel, and he saw Jehu and his company coming and reported what he saw to Jehoram. Jehoram commanded that a horseman be sent to meet them and ask them whether they came for good. This was because Jehoram wanted to be reassured that Ramoth remained in the hands of his soldiers and that Hazael had not been able to recover it from them.

9.15.0.en: A horseman went from Jehoram to find out who was coming and to ask them for news and peace. When he reached Jehu and asked him, Jehu answered him harshly and said to him, "What hast thou to do with peace?" and commanded him to join the soldiers who were with him. The horseman submitted in fear and turned in behind Jehu and joined his soldiers. In this Jehu prevented any news from reaching King Jehoram, so as to surprise him and kill him. The watchman informed King Jehoram that the messenger had not returned to report what he had seen.

9.16.0.en: King Jehoram was alarmed and quickly sent another horseman, and when he reached Jehu, Jehu commanded him too to join his soldiers who were behind him.

9.17.0.en: The king was informed a second time that the second horseman had also not returned. The company had come nearer and nearer to Jehoram's camp, so the watchman could make out the persons, and he recognized Jehu by the way he drove his chariot, for he drove it furiously, and it seems this was known of Jehu, that is, his sharpness, violence and rashness. So the watchman recognized him and told the king.

9.18.0.en: Jehoram's anxiety about Ramoth Gilead increased, and he longed to know its news, especially after the two horsemen he had sent to scout for news did not return, so he went out himself in his chariot, and out of courtesy to him Ahaziah also went out in his chariot to share with him the concern for Ramoth Gilead.

9.18.1.en: This shows the extent of the ignorance and foolishness into which a person falls because of his evil: in pride he thought that Ramoth must remain with him, so he was not on guard and did not understand the danger coming upon him.

9.18.2.en: In proportion to your humility and your prayers, God reveals everything to you and protects you from dangers and the devil's tricks. So take care to pray, to learn from those around you and to consult the Fathers, and you will keep your humility and your peace.

9.19.0.en: Jehoram hurried to ask Jehu whether his coming was for good. Jehu answered: What good do you expect, so long as the debauchery of your mother Jezebel and her witchcrafts prevail? By the harlotry of Jezebel is meant her spiritual adultery, that is, her worship of idols and her abandonment of the worship of God; and by her witchcrafts are meant the pagan acts of worship offered to foreign gods, with all the sorcery, incantations and strange customs they carry.

9.20.0.en: Jehoram turned his chariot the other way, intending to flee, saying to Ahaziah, "There is treachery, O Ahaziah." That is, Jehoram turned back toward Jezreel to escape from the face of Jehu and the army that followed him, and warned Ahaziah to flee as well, because he was certain of the army's rebellion against him under the leadership of Jehu.

9.20.1.en: Although Jehoram cries out, "Treachery," it is at the same time the fulfillment of God's sentence against him because of his evils: even if he escaped from the hand of Hazael, the sword of Jehu would come upon him, as God said to Elijah (1 Kgs 19:17).

9.21.0.en: Jehoram's quickness in fleeing did not help him, for Jehu overtook him with an arrow that pierced his back and went through to his heart, and he fell in his chariot.

9.22.0.en: Captain (third man): one of the three guards accompanying Jehu, that is, one of the closest of those near to him, whom Jehu trusted, who rode with him in his chariot.

9.22.1.en: Jehu said to Bidkar, one of his chief commanders: "Take him up and cast him into the field of Naboth the Jezreelite, and remember how, when you and I were riding together after Ahab his father, the Lord decreed against him this punishment."

9.22.2.en: Thus God's judgment and punishment are carried out upon Ahab, who killed Naboth the Jezreelite, and he perishes, with his son Jehoram, in the very place that he unjustly seized and whose owner he killed.

9.22.3.en: Know that God sees all your deeds, so do not wrong anyone, whatever authority you have, for God defends His weak children. Rather, give every person his right, lest God take vengeance on you.

9.23.0.en: Jehu repeated the word of God, but briefly, giving the meaning without the text, when he declared Ahab's punishment for seizing the field of Naboth and killing him. God defended the weak and told Ahab that He saw the blood of the wronged Naboth and the blood of his sons. It is understood from this that Jezebel had also killed Naboth's sons, so that they would not avenge their father and there would be no heir to Naboth; and God commanded that in the same place Ahab and his descendant, who is Jehoram, would die. His saying "his little field" is a diminutive of field, and this shows the extent of Ahab's injustice, to kill innocent people in order to seize a small field. It is the height of injustice for a person to make light of the lives of others to satisfy his desires.

9.23.1.en: And here we see Jehu hiding behind the word of the Lord by repeating the phrase "the Lord commanded," but in truth he is carrying out his own ambitions and his resentment of Jehoram and his desire for domination and possession.

9.24.0.en: The garden house: it is present-day Jenin, fourteen kilometers southeast of Megiddo, at the southern edge of the valley of Jezreel. It appears that the garden was among the possessions of Ahab, next to which was the field of Naboth.

9.24.1.en: Ibleam: the name of a place west of the river Jordan; its place today is the village of Bal'a, at a distance of seven kilometers south of Jenin and twenty kilometers northeast of Samaria.

9.24.2.en: Megiddo: it is present-day Tell al-Mutasallim, located at a distance of thirty-two kilometers southeast of Haifa. As for Ahaziah king of Judah, who saw what happened, he too fled, by the way of the garden house, and Jehu and his men pursued him, and Jehu commanded them to strike him, so they struck him in his chariot at the ascent of Gur, which is by Ibleam. His wounds were mortal, and he died at Megiddo.

9.24.3.en: The book of Chronicles (2 Chr 22:9) tells us that Ahaziah fled to Samaria, and Jehu's men caught him there and brought him to Megiddo, where Jehu was staying, and killed him there. So the addition made by the book of Chronicles is that he fled first to Samaria before dying at Megiddo, as the second book of Kings tells us.

9.25.0.en: After Ahaziah was killed, his men carried his body and took it to Jerusalem and buried him there in the tombs of the kings, in the city of David, in a tomb that he had prepared for himself. Thus Ahaziah died because of his association with the wicked, that is, the house of Ahab, but he was less wicked than they, so God allowed him to be buried in the city of David and his body not to be thrown to the beasts of the earth and the birds of heaven, like Jehoram the son of Ahab.

9.25.1.en: God appreciates every deed you do, whether good, and He rewards you for it with many blessings, or evil, and He punishes you for it; but if you repent of it and confess and partake of the Holy Mysteries, He removes it from you. So take care to repent, for it is the way of your salvation, and you will have a place in heaven.

9.26.0.en: Ahaziah had become king over Judah in the eleventh year of the reign of Joram the son of Ahab over Israel.

9.26.1.en: As we mentioned, fractions of a year were not counted here, whereas in (ch. 8:25) fractions of a year were counted, so it said the twelfth year of Joram.

9.27.0.en: Jehu entered Jezreel, and Jezebel heard of it, so she painted her eyes and adorned her hair, wanting to show Jehu that she was not afraid of him, for she still had authority, and she looked out of the window. Here the hardness of her heart and her selfishness appear: she was not moved by the death of her son Jehoram and her grandson Ahaziah, and she took care to adorn herself.

9.28.0.en: When Jehu arrived, she greeted him with mocking words, saying to him, "Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?"

9.28.1.en: By this she was hinting to remind him of Zimri king of Israel, who killed Baasha, the king before him, and Zimri remained in power only seven days (1 Kgs 16:9, 10), and then he too was killed in a conspiracy, as though she were telling him that his fate would be like the fate of Zimri. These words carried all the scorn she had toward him and the intense pride that was in her heart, and perhaps she wanted to frighten him.

9.29.0.en: Jehu looked up to the window from which she was addressing him and cried out, "Who is on my side? who?" By this he meant to gather the guards and the eunuchs to follow him, as the new king, and rebel against Jezebel, or else they would be exposed to being killed by his hand. Two or three eunuchs looked out to him, and he commanded them to throw her down from the window, and they threw her down, and her blood splashed on the wall and on the horses, and he trampled her with his horses. This means that she struck the wall of the palace, so her blood ran down the wall, and then Jehu advanced with his horses and trampled her. This shows the extent of Jehu's fierceness, brutality and boldness, for he is not only carrying out the word of God, but shows the extent of the wrath in his heart, which he bore against the house of Ahab.

9.30.0.en: After Jehu trampled Jezebel and killed her, he entered the king's palace, where she used to live, and ate of the food that had been prepared for her and for her son King Jehoram, for he was hard-hearted, sensual and fierce. After he had eaten he said to his men, "Take up the body of Jezebel." He described her as cursed, because of her clinging to the worship of Baal and her seducing her husband Ahab, her sons and her grandsons to worship idols, and her sons and grandsons had become kings over the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah; that is, she corrupted the people of God in both kingdoms and persecuted the prophets of God, especially Elijah, so she became a symbol of evil throughout history, as the Book of Revelation confirms (Rev 2:20). Jehu asked his men to bury her in a tomb, because she was the daughter of a king, who was the king of the Sidonians; that is, he tried to honor her after he had gotten rid of her. In this he shows that he is not carrying out the word of God but his personal purposes, because God had commanded through the mouth of Elijah that Jezebel would be thrown in the field and the dogs would lick up her blood. He confirmed this a second time through the mouth of one of the sons of the prophets, who informed Jehu of it.

9.31.0.en: When they went out to bury her, they found of her remains only the skull, the feet and the palms of her hands, because the dogs had eaten her flesh.

9.32.0.en: Dung: manure, that is, the droppings of animals.

9.32.1.en: When Jehu's men returned, they told him what they had found, and he commented on it, saying: This is the fulfillment of what the Lord decreed by the tongue of Elijah the Tishbite, saying, "The dogs shall eat the flesh of Jezebel in the field of Jezreel, and her body shall be as dung upon the field of Jezreel, so that no one will be able to recognize her, and say, This is Jezebel.

9.32.2.en: The sad end of Jezebel reminds us of the eternal torment that is the end of the wicked. When you remember the judgment every day, you fear God and keep away from sin, however attractive it may seem, for its end is destruction, and so you save your soul and live in repentance and find your life.
